what-is-ai.title: What AI actually is
what-is-ai.description: A worked example of the only thing that separates AI software from ordinary software: the rules are fitted from data.

steps.heading: Two ways to build the same feature
steps.caption: The task — decide whether an email is spam. A human can do it; the question is whether you can write the rules down.

steps.heading: Rule maintenance versus spam catch rate over one year
steps.caption: Rules break — spammers write "F R E E" and the rule misses it. Every patch adds a rule, and the rule set grows faster than the coverage.

steps.heading: Training data: input → label
steps.caption: Learning instead — collect examples with the answer attached. The labelled pairs are the specification; nobody writes the rule.

steps.heading: "Your account is on hold — verify now"
steps.caption: Prediction — a new, unseen email arrives and the model outputs a probability, not a certainty. Thresholding that probability is a product decision.

steps.heading: The lifecycle you are actually operating
steps.caption: Oversight — the model is scored on held-out email it never trained on, and monitored after launch because spam keeps changing.

machine-learning.title: Machine learning: three ways to learn
machine-learning.description: Supervised, unsupervised and reinforcement learning differ in what signal is available, not in how clever they are.

steps.heading: House price prediction
steps.caption: Supervised learning — every example arrives with the right answer attached. The model is corrected directly against it.

steps.heading: Shopper behaviour, unlabelled
steps.caption: Unsupervised learning — no labels exist. The algorithm can only find structure: groups, directions, densities.

steps.heading: An agent learning a maze
steps.caption: Reinforcement learning — no correct action is ever shown. The agent tries something and receives a scalar reward, sometimes much later.

steps.heading: Error during training
steps.caption: Generalisation is the real goal — training error always falls. The number that matters is error on data the model has never seen.

steps.heading: Hiring screen trained on 10 years of past decisions
steps.caption: Inherited bias — the model reproduces the statistics of its data, including the ones you did not intend to teach it.

deep-learning.title: Deep learning: composed representations
deep-learning.description: Why stacking layers helps — each layer builds features out of the layer below it.

steps.heading: A face photo enters as 150,528 raw numbers
steps.caption: Raw input — pixels, with no structure attached. A single linear layer can only draw one straight boundary through this.

steps.heading: Layer 1 features
steps.caption: Shallow layers learn local detectors — edges and colour gradients. These are found automatically, not hand-designed.

steps.heading: Layer 2 features
steps.caption: Middle layers compose them — corners and textures are combinations of edges, and parts are combinations of those.

steps.heading: Layer 3 features and the prediction head
steps.caption: Deep layers reach task concepts — whole faces. The same hierarchy appears in language: characters → words → phrases → intent.

steps.heading: What depth costs
steps.caption: The price — depth needs data and compute, and the learned features are hard to interpret. Depth bought capability, not clarity.

neural-networks.title: One neuron, then a network
neural-networks.description: The whole computation, with real arithmetic: weighted sum, add a bias, apply a nonlinearity.

steps.heading: Input vector x
steps.caption: Inputs — three numbers describing one example. Text, pixels and audio all reduce to a vector like this.

steps.heading: Weights w (learned)
steps.caption: Weights — one learnable number per input, deciding how much that input matters and in which direction. These are what training changes.

steps.heading: Contributions to the pre-activation z
steps.caption: Weighted sum plus bias — each input is multiplied by its weight and everything is added, including a learned offset b = -0.3.

steps.heading: φ(z) for three common activations
steps.caption: Activation — a nonlinearity is applied. ReLU keeps positives and zeroes negatives, so this unit outputs 0: it stays silent.

steps.heading: Same unit, repeated
steps.caption: Scale it — a layer is thousands of these units side by side, and a model is dozens of layers. "7 billion parameters" counts every w and b.

what-is-generative-ai.title: Generative AI: sampling from a learned distribution
what-is-generative-ai.description: The defining behaviour — the same input can produce different valid outputs, because the model samples rather than looks up.

steps.heading: Discriminative output: p(label | email)
steps.caption: A classifier picks from a fixed, tiny set of answers — here two. Its whole output space was defined by you in advance.

steps.heading: Generative output: p(next token | "Write a refund email.")  — top 5 of 50,257
steps.caption: A generator outputs a distribution over its entire vocabulary — tens of thousands of options — and then draws one.

steps.heading: One draw
steps.caption: Sampling — a token is drawn according to those probabilities. This run drew " Hi", the second-most-likely option, entirely legitimately.

steps.heading: Same prompt, three samples
steps.caption: Three runs, three outputs — all fluent, all consistent with the prompt, and one of them contains an invented policy detail.

steps.heading: One idea, several output types
steps.caption: The same mechanism across media — text samples tokens, diffusion samples images, audio models sample waveforms. All draw from a fitted distribution.

discriminative-vs-generative.title: Discriminative vs generative
discriminative-vs-generative.description: One learns where the boundary is. The other learns where the data lives — which is why only one of them can make new examples.

steps.heading: Cats and dogs as feature vectors
steps.caption: The data — labelled examples of two classes in some feature space. Both approaches start here.

steps.heading: p(y | x): a decision boundary
steps.caption: Discriminative — the model only needs the surface that separates the classes. Everything away from that surface is wasted effort.

steps.heading: p(x | y): density per class
steps.caption: Generative — the model instead learns where each class's data is dense. That is a description of the class, not just a wall between classes.

steps.heading: Draw a fresh point from p(x | cat)
steps.caption: Sampling — because the density is known, new points can be drawn from it. This is the capability a boundary can never provide.

steps.heading: A moderation-and-rewrite pipeline
steps.caption: In practice you use both — a classifier to route or filter, a generator to draft. Real products are hybrids.

transformers-overview.title: Inside a transformer block
transformers-overview.description: The repeating unit that everything else in this category expands on.

steps.heading: Before the first block
steps.caption: Input — text becomes token IDs, each ID becomes a vector, and a position signal is added.

steps.heading: Inside block k
steps.caption: Attention sublayer — tokens read from each other. This is the only place in the whole architecture where positions interact.

steps.heading: Inside block k, second half
steps.caption: Feed-forward sublayer — each token is refined on its own by a wide MLP. Communication, then computation.

steps.heading: A 7B-class model: 32 identical blocks
steps.caption: Stack — the identical block repeats N times. Depth is where the architecture gets its capacity.

steps.heading: Logits at the last position, top 4 of 50,257
steps.caption: Output head — the final vector at each position is multiplied by the unembedding matrix to give one score per vocabulary token.

foundation-models.title: One base, many adaptations
foundation-models.description: What "foundation model" buys you, priced against the alternatives.

steps.heading: Where the compute goes
steps.caption: Pretraining — one very expensive run over broad data produces a base model with general capabilities and no particular job.

steps.heading: Tutoring assistant
steps.caption: Adaptation route 1: prompting — the base is untouched. You change behaviour by changing what enters the context window.

steps.heading: Support bot over 50 product manuals
steps.caption: Adaptation route 2: retrieval — still zero training. You attach a searchable document store and inject evidence at query time.

steps.heading: On-brand copy generator (LoRA fine-tune)
steps.caption: Adaptation route 3: fine-tuning — a small fraction of parameters is trained on your data to change style or format reliably.

steps.heading: What you inherit with the base
steps.caption: The trade-off — one shared base means shared strengths and shared inherited flaws, and bigger is not automatically better for your task.

llms.title: What makes a language model "large"
llms.description: The training stages that turn a next-token predictor into an assistant, and what each stage can and cannot fix.

steps.heading: The base model after pretraining
steps.caption: Stage 1, pretraining — predict the next token across trillions of tokens of text. Every capability starts as a side effect of this one objective.

steps.heading: After supervised fine-tuning
steps.caption: Stage 2, instruction tuning — training on curated request/response pairs teaches the model that a prompt is a task, not a prefix.

steps.heading: Multi-step arithmetic accuracy versus training compute (illustrative shape)
steps.caption: Emergent capability — abilities the objective never mentioned appear as scale grows, then plateau. Scale is a lever, not a guarantee.

steps.heading: Six requests to the same model
steps.caption: What scale does not fix — the model still has a knowledge cutoff and no access to your private or live data.

steps.heading: What ships
steps.caption: Stage 3, the application layer — retrieval, tools, guardrails and evaluation sit around the model. That is where products are actually built.

multimodal-intro.title: Multimodal models
multimodal-intro.description: How a picture ends up in the same sequence as words, so one attention stack can relate them.

steps.heading: Two incompatible inputs
steps.caption: Input — an image plus a question. They are completely different data types, so they cannot yet share a sequence.

steps.heading: The image cut into a grid of fixed-size patches
steps.caption: Patching — the image is cut into a grid of fixed-size patches. Each patch will become one sequence element.

steps.heading: Getting pixels into the sequence
steps.caption: Vision encoder and projection — each patch becomes a vector, then a learned matrix maps it into the language model's dimension.

steps.heading: What the language model actually receives
steps.caption: One sequence — visual tokens and text tokens sit side by side. From here it is ordinary self-attention across both.

steps.heading: Two answers to the same photo
steps.caption: Grounding is still not guaranteed — the model can describe details the image does not contain, exactly as it invents text facts.

diffusion-intro.title: Diffusion: learning to undo noise
diffusion-intro.description: The image is not drawn. It is uncovered, one denoising step at a time, from a field of pure noise.

steps.heading: A training image, progressively noised (left to right in ᾱ)
steps.caption: Training, forward process — take a real image and add a known amount of Gaussian noise. The network's job is to predict the noise that was added.

steps.heading: Step 0 of 30
steps.caption: Sampling starts at pure noise — no image, no structure. ᾱ ≈ 0.02, so almost all of the signal is noise.

steps.heading: Step 10 of 30 · prompt: "a glowing orb"
steps.caption: Conditioning — the prompt is embedded and fed into every denoising step, steering which structure emerges. Coarse shapes appear first.

steps.heading: Step 22 of 30
steps.caption: Refinement — later steps remove less noise each time, so the remaining changes are fine detail rather than layout.

steps.heading: Step 30 of 30
steps.caption: Final image — the same iterative loop, run to ᾱ ≈ 1. Fewer steps means faster and rougher; more steps costs latency.
